'''Marina Evseevna Ratner''' ({{langx|ru|Мари́на Евсе́евна Ра́тнер}}; October 30, 1938 – July 7, 2017<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://math.berkeley.edu/people/past-department-members/memoriam/marina-ratner|title=Marina Ratner|website=Department of Mathematics at University of California Berkeley}}</ref>) was a professor of mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] who worked in [[ergodic theory]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/ratner.htm|title=Marina Ratner|last=Larry Riddle|website=agnesscott.edu|access-date=2020-03-24}}</ref> Around 1990, she proved a group of major theorems concerning [[unipotent]] [[flow (mathematics)|flows]] on [[homogeneous space]]s, known as [[Ratner's theorems]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Morris | first=Dave | title=Ratner's theorems on unipotent flows | publisher=University of Chicago Press | location=Chicago | year=2005 | isbn=0-226-53983-0 | ol=OL10192523M | citeseerx=10.1.1.240.9520 | url=http://people.uleth.ca/~dave.morris/lectures/Ratner/Ratner-v1-1.pdf | archive-date=2020-07-09 | access-date=2010-10-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200709191422/http://people.uleth.ca/~dave.morris/lectures/Ratner/Ratner-v1-1.pdf | url-status=dead }}</ref> Ratner was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1992,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/multimedia/pdfs/classlist.pdf|title=LIST OF ACTIVE MEMBERS BY CLASS|last=|first=|date=October 27, 2016|website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|language=en|access-date=2020-03-24}}</ref> awarded the [[Ostrowski Prize]] in 1993 and elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] the same year. In 1994, she was awarded the [[John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science|John J. Carty Award]] from the National Academy of Sciences.<ref name=Carty>{{cite web|title=John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science |url=http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_carty |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |accessdate=25 February 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229180532/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_carty |archivedate=29 December 2010 }}</ref>

== Early life ==

Ratner was born October 30, 1938, in [[Moscow]], [[Russian SFSR]]. Her father was a plant physiologist and professor, and her mother was a chemist. Her family suffered from discrimination and [[antisemitism]] because they were Jewish. Ratner's mother was fired from work in the 1940s for writing to her mother in Israel, then considered an enemy of the Soviet state.<ref name="third" />

Ratner gained an interest in mathematics in her fifth grade.<ref name="third" /> She was able to go to [[Moscow State University]] because the university had limited discrimination against Jewish applicants as the [[Nikita Khrushchev|Khrushchev]] era began.<ref name=":0" />

From 1956 to 1961, Ratner studied mathematics and physics at Moscow State University. Here, she became interested in [[probability theory]], inspired by [[Andrey Kolmogorov|A.N. Kolmogorov]] and his group.<ref name="third">{{Cite web|url=http://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Ratner.html|title=Marina Ratner biography|website=[[mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk]]|access-date=2019-02-09}}</ref>

== Career ==
After graduation, Ratner spent four years working in Kolmogorov's applied statistics group. Following this, she returned to Moscow State university for graduate studies under [[Yakov Sinai|Yakov G. Sinai]], also a student of Kolmogorov. She completed her PhD thesis, titled "Geodesic Flows on Unit Tangent Bundles of Compact Surfaces of Negative Curvature", in 1969.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=32902}}</ref> During this time, Ratner studied the aforementioned [[geodesic flow]]s as well as a special class of flows called [[Anosov flow]]s. After earning her doctorate, she worked at the High Technical Engineering School in Moscow until she lost her job in 1970 due to applying for an emigration visa to Israel.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Dani |first=S. G. |date=2019-03-01 |title=Marina Ratner (1938–2017) |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/201903/rnoti-p368.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=66 |issue=03 |pages=1 |doi=10.1090/noti1835  |doi-access=free|issn=0002-9920}}</ref>

In 1971 Ratner emigrated from the Soviet Union to Israel and she taught at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] from 1971 until 1975. She continued to study geodesic flows, extending her results to higher dimensions. Ratner also proved that the trajectory of Anosov flows exhibited the Bernoulli property of randomness. She began to work with [[Rufus Bowen]] at Berkeley, who was studying similar [[Axiom A]] flows, and eventually was invited to join him as a professor in 1975.<ref name=":0" /> Ratner then emigrated to the United States and became a professor of mathematics at Berkeley, with "some controversy" following within the department.<ref name=":0" /> Ratner studied [[horocycle flow]]s, proving that they are "loosely Bernoulli", and their [[Cartesian square]]s are not. In the early 1980s she described how [[Rigidity (mathematics)|rigidity]] applied to horocycle flows, and this led to her work on the Raghunathan conjecture.<ref name=":0" />

During the 1980s Ratner published proofs of conjectures dealing with [[unipotent]] flows on quotients of [[Lie group]]s made by [[S. G. Dani]] and [[M. S. Raghunathan]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Cook | first=Mariana | title=Mathematicians : an outer view of the inner world | publisher=Princeton University Press | location=Princeton, N.J | year=2009 | isbn=978-0-691-13951-7 | ol=OL23694032M }}</ref> During this time she proved a property now named after her, showing that two unipotent flow trajectories that remain together for a period of time will remain close for a much longer time.<ref name=":0" />

In 1986, she boycotted the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] hosted in [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]] for its “de facto ‘female free’ policy.”<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barany |first=Michael |date=2026 |title=A Very Brief Political History of American-hosted International Congresses of Mathematicians |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202604/rnoti-p289a.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=73 |issue=04 |doi=10.1090/noti3314  |doi-access=free|issn=1088-9477}}</ref>

Much of Ratner's work focused on [[dynamical system]]s, especially over [[homogeneous space]]s. Her results were abstract and had extensive consequences for different fields within math. In particular, a wide array of research in [[number theory]] has proceeded from her results.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Ng-Yu |first=Maya |date=2017-07-28 |title=Professor emeritus, acclaimed mathematician Marina Ratner dies at 78 |url=https://www.dailycal.org/2017/07/27/professor-emeritus-acclaimed-mathematician-marina-ratner-dies-78/ |access-date=2019-12-20 |website=The Daily Californian |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Before earning her doctorate, Ratner had a daughter, Anna, from a brief marriage.<ref name=":0" />

Ratner moved to Israel with her parents in the early 1970s. Her sister Judith remained in the Soviet Union, and lost her job as a research metallurgist in 1973 due to her family's emigration. When Ratner later moved to the U.S., her parents stayed in Israel. Judith applied to leave the Soviet Union in 1977 along with her husband, but they were denied permission and faced persecution because they were Jewish. Judith's family eventually received permission to leave in 1987.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=http://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/12/03/Soviet-refusenik-to-be-released/2923565506000/|title=Soviet refusenik to be released|last=Hartsock|first=John|date=1987-12-03
|work=UPI|language=en}}</ref>

Marina Ratner died July 7, 2017, at the age of 78.<ref name=":1" />

== Honors and legacy ==
In 1992, Ratner was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and in 1993, the National Academy of Sciences.<ref name="third" /> Ratner also won the Ostrowski prize in 1993.<ref name=":0" /> For her theorems on unipotent flows and other work, she won the [[John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science]] in 1994.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/john-j-carty-award.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111126045126/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/john-j-carty-award.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 26, 2011|title=John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science|website=nasonline.org|access-date=2019-02-09}}</ref> Also that year, she became the third woman plenary speaker at International Congress of Mathematicians, and [[Ingrid Daubechies]] followed her at the same conference. [[Emmy Noether]] and [[Karen Uhlenbeck]] had been the only other women to speak there for decades. Ratner's talk was titled ''Interactions between ergodic theory, Lie groups and number theory.''<ref name="third" /> In 2004, Ratner won the Donald Sterling Noyce Prize for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching.<ref name=":1" />

In 2013, Ratner received an honorary doctorate from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and they hosted a conference about her work.<ref name=":0" />

Some mathematicians claim that Ratner would have won the [[Fields Medal]], the most prestigious prize in mathematics, if her work had been completed by the age of 40, as required by the prize. [[Elon Lindenstrauss]] and [[Maryam Mirzakhani]] won the Fields Medal for work that grew out of Ratner's results.<ref name=":1" /> Her discoveries influenced many fields of mathematics, including geometry, dynamics, [[diophantine approximation]], [[ergodic theory]], and Lie group theory.<ref name=":0" />
